# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# list-products.contract.yaml
#
# Normative, externally observable specification of the "list products"
# functionality. It sits beside the design note for the same feature: the
# design note says how and why, this file says what is true from the outside.
#
# ONE FILE, TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS. This file is not duplicated per side. Two thin
# harnesses read it (see `verification.harnesses`):
#
#   server harness : seeds the catalogue with `fixtures[case.fixture]`, replays
#                    `case.http.request` against the running server, asserts
#                    `case.http.response`.
#   client harness : starts a stub HTTP server that asserts the incoming request
#                    equals `case.http.request` and replies with
#                    `case.http.response`; invokes `case.call` on the client and
#                    asserts `case.result`.
#
# A case with `applies_to: [server]` is skipped by the client harness and vice
# versa. Both harnesses must report the set of case ids they executed; CI fails
# if the union is not the full set of ids in `cases`.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

contract: list-products
version: 1.0.0
status: normative
last_updated: 2026-07-31

description: >
  Retrieval of a paginated, filtered, deterministically ordered page of the
  product catalogue, as observed over HTTP by any caller, and as observed at
  the client library's public operation boundary.

scope:
  in_scope:
    - the HTTP request the client is allowed to produce for a given call
    - the HTTP response the server is required to produce for a given request
    - the value or error the client is required to surface for a given response
    - ordering, pagination, filtering and error semantics
  out_of_scope:
    - authentication and authorisation
    - rate limiting, caching headers, compression
    - persistence, transport internals, logging, metrics
    - how products enter the catalogue

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
verification:

  harnesses:
    server: >
      For each case where "server" is in applies_to: reset the catalogue to
      fixtures[case.fixture], issue case.http.request verbatim, assert
      case.http.response under `matching`.
    client: >
      For each case where "client" is in applies_to: stand up a stub endpoint,
      invoke the operation named in case.call with exactly the arguments listed
      (arguments absent from the list must not be passed at all), assert that
      exactly case.expected_requests HTTP requests were made and that the first
      one matches case.http.request, reply with case.http.response, then assert
      case.result.

  naming: >
    Field names in this file are snake_case and are the names on the wire. A
    client written in a language with a different convention may expose
    idiomatic names, provided the mapping is purely mechanical (snake_case to
    the target convention) and is applied by the harness, not by hand per case.

  matching:
    request:
      method: exact
      path: exact
      query: >
        exact set of decoded key/value pairs; parameter order is irrelevant;
        a repeated parameter is a failure; absent means the parameter must not
        appear at all, not that it may appear empty
      headers: listed headers only, names case-insensitive, values exact
      body: must be absent
    response:
      status: exact
      headers: listed headers only, names case-insensitive, values exact
      body: >
        parsed as JSON then compared deeply; object keys are strict (an extra
        key is a failure); array order is significant; numbers must be JSON
        integers where the schema says integer
    result: deep equality on the listed fields; extra fields are a failure

  placeholders:
    "<any:non-empty-string>": matches any JSON string of length >= 1
    "<same-as:http.response.body>": >
      matches the decoded response body of the same case, field for field

  success_shorthand: >
    For every 200 case the client's return value is the decoded response body,
    field for field, with no re-ordering, re-formatting or defaulting. Success
    cases therefore carry no explicit `result` block: the expectation is the
    response body already written in the case. Only non-200 cases spell out
    `result`.

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
interface:

  http:
    method: GET
    path: /products
    request_headers:
      accept: application/json
    query_parameters:
      page:
        type: integer
        constraint: ">= 1"
        default: 1
      page_size:
        type: integer
        constraint: "1 <= n <= 100"
        default: 20
      category:
        type: string
        constraint: "non-empty; exact, case-sensitive match"
        default: null
      q:
        type: string
        constraint: "1 to 100 characters"
        default: null
      sort:
        type: enum
        values: ["name", "-name", "price_cents", "-price_cents"]
        default: "name"
      in_stock:
        type: enum
        values: ["true", "false"]
        default: null

  client_operation:
    name: listProducts
    arguments: [page, page_size, category, q, sort, in_stock]
    returns: page  # see schemas.page
    raises: [ValidationError, ApiError, ServerError, TransportError]

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
schemas:

  product:
    id: {type: string}
    name: {type: string}
    price_cents: {type: integer, constraint: ">= 0"}
    currency: {type: string, constraint: "ISO 4217, uppercase"}
    category: {type: string}
    in_stock: {type: boolean}

  page:
    items: {type: array, of: product}
    page: {type: integer}
    page_size: {type: integer}
    total: {type: integer}

  error:
    error:
      code: {type: string}
      field: {type: string, nullable: true}
      message: {type: string, note: "human readable; never asserted"}

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rules:

  - id: R-01
    text: Absent page defaults to 1 and absent page_size defaults to 20.

  - id: R-02
    text: >
      Ordering is total and stable across identical requests: primary key is
      `sort` ("name" and "-name" compare case-insensitively), ties are broken
      by `id` ascending in byte order.

  - id: R-03
    text: >
      `total` is the number of products matching the filters, independent of
      pagination. `page` and `page_size` echo the effective values.

  - id: R-04
    text: A page past the last one is valid — 200 with an empty `items` array.

  - id: R-05
    text: category, q and in_stock combine with AND.

  - id: R-06
    text: >
      `q` matches a case-insensitive substring of `name` only; no other field
      participates and no fuzzy or token matching is performed.

  - id: R-07
    text: Unknown query parameters are ignored by the server.

  - id: R-08
    text: >
      An invalid parameter value yields 400 with error.code = "invalid_argument"
      and error.field naming the first offending parameter in this precedence
      order: page, page_size, category, q, sort, in_stock.

  - id: R-09
    text: >
      Prices are integers in the currency's minor unit. Neither side may emit
      them as floats or strings, and neither side rounds, scales or formats.

  - id: R-10
    text: >
      The client performs no local validation and no local defaulting: it sends
      exactly the arguments it was given and nothing else, and every call
      produces exactly one HTTP request. There are no retries, on any status.

  - id: R-11
    text: >
      Client status mapping: 200 -> return the decoded body; 400 ->
      ValidationError(code, field, status); other 4xx -> ApiError(code, status);
      5xx -> ServerError(status); no response, a truncated response or a body
      that is not valid JSON -> TransportError.

  - id: R-12
    text: Every response carries `content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8`.

  - id: R-13
    text: An empty result is 200 with an empty array, never 404.

  - id: R-14
    text: The request is safe and idempotent and carries no body.

  - id: R-15
    text: Any method other than GET on /products yields 405 with `allow: GET`.

I chose a declarative YAML contract rather than prose or Gherkin because the two implementations sit on opposite sides of the same wire, and only a data file can be *read* by two different harnesses in two different languages without either side re-stating the expectations in its own words. Each case carries the request, the response and the client-visible outcome together, so the server harness replays it forwards and the client harness replays it backwards against a stub — one fact, two directions of verification. Gherkin would have been just as readable, but its step definitions would have had to be written and kept in sync twice, which is the duplication you asked me to avoid. YAML also keeps the rules, the fixtures and the cases in one reviewable document, with `verifies:` links so a changed rule points straight at the cases that must move with it.

# list-products.spec.yaml
# ============================================================================
# Observable behaviour of "list products".
#
# This file is the single source of truth for BOTH implementations:
#   * the server — must produce these responses for these requests
#   * the client — must produce these requests, and these return values from
#                  these responses
#
# There is deliberately no per-implementation copy. Each side ships a thin
# runner that loads THIS file and executes every case whose `verified_by`
# list contains that side. See `conformance:` at the bottom of the file.
#
# Field types and schemas live in the sibling interface file in this
# directory (see `spec.interface`). That file says what the shapes are;
# this file says what is true from the outside.
#
# Changing behaviour means changing this file first. A change to the server
# or the client that alters anything observable and does not touch this file
# is a bug in the change, not in the spec.
# ============================================================================

spec:
  name: list-products
  version: 3
  interface: ./list-products.openapi.yaml   # ← point at the sibling interface file
  operation: listProducts
  transport:
    method: GET
    path: /v1/products

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# How a runner compares an actual value to an expected value written below.
# Both runners MUST implement this identically; it is the only place matching
# semantics are defined.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
matching:
  objects: exact
    # Every key in the expected object must be present and equal, and the
    # actual object must have no additional keys.
  arrays: ordered-exact
    # Same length, same order, element-wise `objects: exact`.
  headers: subset
    # Only the headers listed are checked. Names are case-insensitive.
    # `content-type` is compared by media type only; parameters such as
    # `; charset=utf-8` are ignored.
  query: decoded-exact
    # Compared as a parsed map of decoded name -> value. Percent-encoding
    # style and parameter order are NOT specified and MUST NOT be asserted.
    # Values are always strings, because that is what a query string carries.
  numbers: exact
  timestamps: exact-string

  placeholders:
    "${any:string}":            any JSON string
    "${any:non-empty-string}":  any JSON string of length >= 1
    "${any:integer}":           any JSON integer
    "${product:<id>}":          the object under fixtures.<active>.products with that id
    "${products:<id>,<id>,…}":  an array of those product objects, in the order written
    "${products:canonical[a:b]}": a slice (half-open, 0-based) of the active
                                fixture's `canonical_order`, expanded to product objects
    "${captured:<name>}":       a value captured by an earlier step of the same case

  defaults:
    fixture: catalog
    returns: >-
      If a case omits both `returns` and `raises`, the client MUST return a page
      value deep-equal to the decoded `http.response.body`.
    query: >-
      If a case omits `http.request.query`, the request MUST carry no query
      parameters at all.
    steps: >-
      A case without `steps` is a one-step case: its top-level `call`, `http`,
      `returns` / `raises` form step 1.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fixtures. The server under test is reset to the named fixture before each
# case. Each product object below is exactly the representation the API
# returns for that product — there is no separate serialisation table.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
fixtures:
  reset: before-each-case

  catalog:
    products:
      - { id: p_001, name: "Mouse Pad",           category: home,        price_cents:   900, status: active,        created_at: "2025-08-01T07:00:00Z" }
      - { id: p_002, name: "USB-C Hub",           category: electronics, price_cents:  4900, status: discontinued,  created_at: "2025-09-30T16:45:00Z" }
      - { id: p_003, name: "Mechanical Keyboard", category: electronics, price_cents: 12900, status: active,        created_at: "2025-11-22T08:15:00Z" }
      - { id: p_004, name: "Monitor Arm",         category: furniture,   price_cents:  8900, status: active,        created_at: "2026-01-05T12:00:00Z" }
      - { id: p_005, name: "Cable Tray",          category: furniture,   price_cents:  2900, status: active,        created_at: "2026-01-05T12:00:00Z" }
      - { id: p_006, name: "Standing Desk",       category: furniture,   price_cents: 49900, status: active,        created_at: "2026-02-19T09:30:00Z" }
      - { id: p_007, name: "Desk Lamp",           category: home,        price_cents:  3400, status: active,        created_at: "2026-03-04T10:00:00Z" }
    # Derived from R2. Stated explicitly so the ordering rule and the cases
    # cannot drift apart. p_004 precedes p_005 on the id tie-break.
    canonical_order: [p_007, p_006, p_004, p_005, p_003, p_002, p_001]

  empty:
    products: []
    canonical_order: []

  wide:
    # 25 products, generated. Only string interpolation is used; `n` runs 1..25
    # and `{n:02}` is `n` zero-padded to two digits.
    generated:
      count: 25
      template:
        id: "w_{n:02}"
        name: "Widget {n:02}"
        category: widgets
        price_cents: 1000
        status: active
        created_at: "2026-01-{n:02}T00:00:00Z"
    canonical_order: descending n  # w_25, w_24, …, w_01

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Normative rules. Every rule must be referenced by at least one case (CI
# checks this). Rules are what a reviewer reads; cases are what a machine runs.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
rules:

  # -- shape of a successful answer -----------------------------------------
  R1: >-
    A successful response is 200 with a JSON object whose keys are exactly
    `items` and `next_cursor`. `next_cursor` is always present; it is `null`
    when there is no further page.
  R2: >-
    Products are ordered by `created_at` descending, ties broken by `id`
    ascending. The order is total and stable: the same catalogue always
    produces the same sequence.
  R3: >-
    When the caller does not specify a page size, at most 20 products are
    returned.
  R4: >-
    `limit` sets the page size. Valid values are integers 1 to 100 inclusive.
  R5: >-
    `next_cursor` is non-null if and only if at least one further product
    matches the same filters after the last item returned.
  R6: >-
    A cursor is opaque. No caller may parse, construct, compare or persist
    meaning into it. Passing a cursor back returns the next page under the
    same filters; the filters are carried by the cursor and need not be
    repeated, but repeating them identically is also valid.
  R7: >-
    Traversal is exactly-once: while the catalogue is unchanged, following the
    cursor chain to its end yields every matching product exactly once, in the
    order of R2, with no gaps and no duplicates — including across a page
    boundary that splits a `created_at` tie.
  R8: >-
    `category` filters by exact, case-sensitive string equality.
  R9: >-
    `status` filters by exact string equality. Absent means no filtering by
    status; discontinued products are returned by default.
  R10: >-
    A request that matches nothing is 200 with `items: []` and
    `next_cursor: null`. It is never 404 and never an error.
  R11: >-
    Unrecognised query parameters are ignored, not rejected.

  # -- errors ----------------------------------------------------------------
  R12: >-
    A `limit` that is not an integer, or is below 1, or above 100, is
    rejected with 400 and error code `INVALID_LIMIT`.
  R13: >-
    A cursor the server cannot interpret — malformed, truncated, or issued for
    a different filter set — is rejected with 400 and code `INVALID_CURSOR`.
  R14: >-
    An error response body is `{"error": {"code": …, "message": …}}`. `code` is
    a stable machine-readable identifier. `message` is human-facing prose: it
    may change at any time and is never asserted by a test.

  # -- client-side obligations ----------------------------------------------
  R15: >-
    The client sends only the parameters the caller supplied. An option the
    caller did not set produces no query parameter, so the server's default
    applies.
  R16: >-
    The client does not validate arguments locally. Out-of-range values are
    sent to the server and the server's error is surfaced to the caller.
  R17: >-
    The client maps outcomes to caller-visible errors as follows:
    400 -> InvalidRequest, carrying the server's `code` verbatim;
    5xx or a transport failure -> Unavailable;
    a 2xx body that is not JSON, or that does not satisfy R1 -> ProtocolError.
  R18: >-
    One call performs exactly one request: no automatic retry, no
    prefetching of the next page, no speculative parallel requests.
  R19: >-
    The client returns `next_cursor` to the caller unchanged and sends a
    caller-supplied cursor back unchanged.
  R20: >-
    Every request carries `Accept: application/json`.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cases. `verified_by` records which sides can observe the case; a case that
# only one side can reach says so, rather than being duplicated or dropped.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
cases:

    title: Default call returns the whole catalogue in canonical order
    rules: [R1, R2, R9, R15, R20]
    verified_by: [server, client]

# How the two sides consume this file.

conformance:

  server:
    for_each_case_where: server in verified_by
    procedure:
      - Reset the catalogue to `case.fixture` (default `catalog`) through the
        adapter's seed hook. How that hook works is the server's business;
        that it exists and is synchronous is not.
      - For each step, send `http.request` verbatim against the running
        service.
      - Assert the actual response against `http.response` using `matching`.
      - Resolve `capture` entries from the ACTUAL response, so later steps use
        real cursors.
    ignores: [call, returns, raises, expect.request_count]

  client:
    for_each_case_where: client in verified_by
    procedure:
      - Start a stub HTTP server for the duration of the case. It records every
        request it receives.
      - For each step, invoke the client with `call.args` through the adapter.
      - Assert the request the stub received against `http.request` using
        `matching`.
      - Reply with `http.response`. Where the response contains an
        `${any:…}` placeholder, the stub substitutes a fixed synthetic value
        (`"stub-cursor-<step>"` for cursors) and records it, so that
        `capture` and `${captured:…}` refer to that concrete value. This is the
        one place where the two runners read the same field differently: the
        server runner treats `http.response` as an assertion, the client runner
        treats it as a script.
      - Assert the value returned, or the error raised, against `returns` /
        `raises`. If both are absent, the return value must deep-equal the
        response body.
      - Assert `expect.request_count` against the stub's record, defaulting to
        one request per step.
    ignores: [fixtures]

  adapter:
    purpose: >-
      The only per-implementation code. It is glue, not specification: it must
      contain no case-specific logic and no conditionals on case ids.
    server_side:
      - seed(fixture) -> void
    client_side:
      - call(op, args) -> page | error
      - normalise(page) -> { items, next_cursor }   # back into wire form
      - classify(error) -> { error: InvalidRequest | Unavailable | ProtocolError,
                             code: string | null }
    note: >-
      Argument and field naming may be idiomatic in each language. The adapter
      is where `next_cursor` becomes `nextCursor` — never this file, and never
      a second copy of it.

  ci:
    - Every rule id appears in at least one case's `rules`.
    - Every case id is reported by every side listed in its `verified_by`.
      A case that is skipped, unknown to a runner, or silently absent fails
      the build; a case that is neither passed nor failed is a failure.
    - Every case excluded from a side carries a `reason_*_excluded`.
    - `fixtures.*.canonical_order` agrees with R2 applied to

Keeping the normative `rules` as numbered prose alongside the machine-readable `cases` means a human reviewer can argue about the intent while CI checks that every rule is actually exercised. The `verified_by` field is the honest part: a client cannot send `limit=abc` and a server cannot map a socket error to `Unavailable`, so asymmetry is recorded in the one file instead of being duplicated away.

about: |
  WHAT THIS FILE IS
  This file describes only what an outside observer can see: the HTTP exchange
  and the value returned by the client library. It never mentions databases,
  caches, ORMs, frameworks, file layout, or function names of either
  implementation. Every statement here is either a `rule` (prose, normative) or
  a `case` (data, machine-checkable). Every rule is covered by at least one
  case; that invariant is itself checked (see `verification.meta_checks`).

    seed `given.catalog`, send `request`, assert the reply matches `response`.

# skip it via `roles`). CI fails if either harness reports a case as "unknown".
# =============================================================================

meta:
  contract: list-products
  version: 1.3.0            # bump minor for added cases, major for changed ones
  operation: list_products  # canonical operation name used by the client binding
  shape_reference: ./list-products.openapi.yaml   # types & schemas live there
  owns: >-
    Ordering, pagination, filtering, defaults, error semantics, tolerance rules.
    Field types and required-ness are owned by the shape reference and are not
    re-stated here.

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. How a runner executes this file
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
conformance:
  roles:
    provider:
      runs_cases_with_role: [provider]
      procedure:
        - Reset the product store and load `case.fixture` verbatim.
        - For each step, send `request` exactly as written (no added query params).
        - Assert response `status` (exact).
        - Assert response `headers` (listed headers must be present and equal;
          header names case-insensitive; extra headers allowed).
        - Assert response `body` (deep equality after matcher resolution,
          unless the step sets `body_match: subset`).
        - Array order is significant everywhere in this file.
    consumer:
      runs_cases_with_role: [consumer]
      procedure:
        - Programme the transport double with the step's `response`
          (or `response_script` for multi-attempt steps).
        - Invoke `meta.operation` with `client.args`; omitted args mean
          "caller did not supply this argument", not "supply null".
        - Assert the emitted HTTP request: `method` and `path` exact,
          query parameters exact as a set (no extras, no omissions),
          `headers` as a subset, and no request body.
        - Assert `client.returns` (deep equality of the value normalised to
          canonical JSON per `bindings.normalisation`) or `client.raises`.
  independence: >-
    Cases are independent and may run in any order or in parallel. Steps inside
    one case are ordered and share captured variables.
  variables:
    capture: "capture: {name: <path>} stores a value after a step succeeds."
    reference: "${var:name} resolves to a captured value."
  matchers:
    "${any:string}": any JSON string
    "${any:nonempty_string}": any JSON string of length >= 1
    "${any:integer}": any JSON integer
    "${any:rfc3339}": any RFC 3339 timestamp string with a UTC offset
    "${absent}": the key must not be present at all
    null: the key must be present with JSON null

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Language bindings (the only per-implementation code that may exist)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
bindings:
  rule: >-
    Each implementation ships an adapter of at most ~100 lines. Adapters
    translate names and types; they may not contain expected values, and they
    may not skip, reorder, or reinterpret cases.
  arg_names: [limit, cursor, status, q]
  normalisation: >-
    The client's return value is normalised to canonical JSON before comparison:
    money stays an integer number of minor units, timestamps are serialised as
    RFC 3339 in UTC ("Z"), and optional/absent values become JSON null.
  error_mapping:
    # canonical error name  ->  what the client must surface
    invalid_argument: "an error carrying code=invalid_argument and the field name"
    invalid_cursor: "an error carrying code=invalid_cursor"
    cursor_context_mismatch: "an error carrying code=cursor_context_mismatch"
    server_error: "a distinct error type, never a parse/validation error"
    timeout: "a distinct timeout error type"

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Normative rules. Every rule must be exercised by >= 1 case (CI-checked).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
rules:
  R-01: "Success is 200 with a body of exactly {items, next_cursor}."
  R-02: "Default order is created_at descending, ties broken by id ascending."
  R-03: "Default limit is 20 when the caller supplies no limit."
  R-04: "limit is the maximum page size; a full page does not imply more pages."
  R-05: "next_cursor is a non-empty opaque string when more items exist, and
         JSON null on the last page. It is never absent and never an empty string."
  R-06: "A cursor is opaque: clients must not parse, build, or mutate it."
  R-07: "Walking every page with a stable store yields every matching item
         exactly once, in the order of R-02."
  R-08: "A cursor is only valid together with the same filter arguments
         (status, q) as the request that produced it; otherwise 400
         cursor_context_mismatch."
  R-09: "status filters by exact value. Absent status means no filtering:
         archived items are included."
  R-10: "q matches case-insensitively as a substring of name OR sku.
         No match is 200 with items: [] and next_cursor: null, never 404."
  R-11: "limit must be an integer in [1, 100]; otherwise 400 invalid_argument
         with field=limit."
  R-12: "A cursor that is not well-formed or not recognised is 400 invalid_cursor."
  R-13: "Unknown query parameters are ignored, not rejected."
  R-14: "Unknown response fields are ignored by the client (forward compatibility)."
  R-15: "The client accepts application/json with or without a charset parameter."
  R-16: "The client retries at most 2 additional times on 502/503/504 and on
         connection errors, with a delay of >= 100 ms between attempts.
         It never retries a 4xx."
  R-17: "Any non-2xx that is not a defined error, and any unparseable body,
         surfaces as server_error - never as a success with empty items."
  R-18: "The client sends Accept: application/json, no request body, and omits
         query parameters the caller did not supply."
  R-19: "Methods other than GET on the collection are 405 with Allow: GET."
  R-20: "The error body is exactly {error: {code, field, message}}; message is
         human-readable, never empty, and never asserted verbatim."

I chose a declarative YAML case table rather than prose or Gherkin because both harnesses need to *read the same expected values as data* — the server replays `request`/`response` pairs while the client replays `response` and checks `client.args`/`returns` — and prose or step definitions would force each side to re-encode those values in its own test code, which is exactly the duplication you want to avoid. YAML keeps the file diffable and reviewable by hand while remaining directly loadable in any language, so the per-implementation code shrinks to a thin name-mapping adapter that contains no expectations. The explicit `roles` field lets genuinely one-sided behaviour (405 handling, retries, unknown-field tolerance) live in the same file instead of leaking into a private test suite. The numbered `rules` plus the `coverage` index make the file auditable: a rule with no case, or a case asserting something no rule states, is a CI failure rather than a silent divergence.

# list_products.contract.yaml
#
# Sibling of the list-products design document. That document explains *why*;
# this file defines *what is observable from outside*, in a form both test
# harnesses execute directly.
#
# This file is the ONLY normative source of list-products behaviour.
# It is consumed twice, unmodified:
#
#   server harness -> boots the service, seeds `fixtures`, replays each case's
#                     `http.request`, asserts `http.response`.
#   client harness -> installs a transport double, invokes `client.call`,
#                     asserts the emitted `http.request`, replies with
#                     `http.response`, asserts `client.returns` / `client.raises`.
#
# Neither harness may hold behavioural knowledge of its own. If a case cannot
# be expressed here, the matcher vocabulary is extended here first.
# =============================================================================

contract: list_products
version: 1
status: normative
media_type: "application/json"

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Matcher vocabulary. The full set of things a harness must understand.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
matchers:
  literal:      "A scalar/array/object compares by value. Arrays are order-significant."
  "$closed":    "Default for every object in `http.response.body`: no unlisted keys allowed."
  "$contains":  "Used for headers: listed entries must match, others are ignored."
  "$opaque":    |
    Value whose content is not specified, only its existence and later reuse.
    server direction: assert non-empty string, bind actual value to the given name.
    client direction: synthesise the declared `sample` into the injected response.
  "$bound":     "Substitute the value bound by an earlier `$opaque` (same run)."
  "$product":   "Expand to the wire projection of the named fixture row (see §2)."
  "$absent":    "Key must not be present."

applies_to_default: [server, client]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Interface surface
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
http:
  method: GET
  path: /v1/products
  request_headers_required:
    Accept: "application/json"
  query_parameters:
    limit:    { type: integer, min: 1, max: 100, default: 20 }
    cursor:   { type: string, opaque: true, default: null }
    category: { type: string, default: null, semantics: "exact match on product.category" }
    q:        { type: string, default: null, semantics: "see rule R-07" }
    sort:
      type: enum
      values: [name_asc, name_desc, price_asc, price_desc]
      default: name_asc
  unknown_query_parameters: ignored
  response_headers:
    Content-Type: "application/json; charset=utf-8"

client:
  # The client exposes one operation. Argument and field names are given in
  # snake_case; an implementation may render them in its language's convention
  # (listProducts / next_cursor -> nextCursor). The mapping must be mechanical
  # and total — no renaming, no dropping, no adding.
  operation: list_products
  arguments: [limit, cursor, category, q, sort]
  returns:
    type: Page
    fields:
      items:       "list of Product, order preserved from the wire"
      next_cursor: "string or null, passed through verbatim"
      has_more:    "derived: next_cursor != null (see R-C3)"
  error_types:
    InvalidRequest: "HTTP 400; carries `code` and `field` from the error body"
    ServerError:    "HTTP 5xx after retries are exhausted"
    ProtocolError:  "2xx whose body is not decodable as the documented shape"
    TransportError: "no HTTP response obtained"

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Fixture catalogue
#
# `_internal` keys exist in the seed data and must never reach the wire (R-03).
# The wire projection of a row is: id, name, category, price, in_stock.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
fixtures:
  catalog_A:
    - { id: p_01, name: "Anvil",          category: tools,   price: { amount_minor: 4999,  currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 3100, supplier_ref: "S-77" } }
    - { id: p_02, name: "apple crate",    category: produce, price: { amount_minor: 1250,  currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 700,  supplier_ref: "S-12" } }
    - { id: p_03, name: "Apple Crate XL", category: produce, price: { amount_minor: 2500,  currency: EUR }, in_stock: false, archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 1500, supplier_ref: "S-12" } }
    - { id: p_04, name: "Bellows",        category: tools,   price: { amount_minor: 8900,  currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 5000, supplier_ref: "S-77" } }
    - { id: p_05, name: "Äpfel",          category: produce, price: { amount_minor: 999,   currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 400,  supplier_ref: "S-12" } }
    - { id: p_06, name: "Zither",         category: music,   price: { amount_minor: 12000, currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 8000, supplier_ref: "S-31" } }
    - { id: p_07, name: "Ghost Widget",   category: tools,   price: { amount_minor: 100,   currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: true,  _internal: { cost_minor: 50,   supplier_ref: "S-77" } }
    - { id: p_08, name: "Bellows",        category: tools,   price: { amount_minor: 8900,  currency: EUR }, in_stock: true,  archived: false, _internal: { cost_minor: 5000, supplier_ref: "S-90" } }

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Rules. Every rule names the cases that check it; a meta-test asserts that
#    `checked_by` is non-empty for each rule and that every id resolves.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
rules:
  R-01:
    text: "A successful response is 200 with body {items, next_cursor} and nothing else."
    checked_by: [LP-01, LP-10, LP-20]
  R-02:
    text: "Each item carries exactly id, name, category, price{amount_minor,currency}, in_stock."
    checked_by: [LP-01]
  R-03:
    text: "Archived rows and `_internal` data are never observable through this endpoint,
            under any parameter combination."
    checked_by: [LP-01, LP-05, LP-06]
  R-04:
    text: "Default order is name_asc: ascending byte comparison of the name's UTF-8 NFC
            encoding. It is therefore case-sensitive and not locale-aware."
    checked_by: [LP-01]
  R-05:
    text: "Ties in any sort are broken by ascending byte comparison of `id`, in that
            direction, regardless of the primary sort direction."
    checked_by: [LP-03, LP-04]
  R-06:
    text: "`category` filters by exact string equality."
    checked_by: [LP-05]
  R-07:
    text: "`q` is a substring match on name, folding ASCII A-Z/a-z only. Non-ASCII
            characters are compared as-is."
    checked_by: [LP-06, LP-07]
  R-08:
    text: "A query matching nothing returns 200, empty items, next_cursor null — not 404."
    checked_by: [LP-08]
  R-09:
    text: "Paging is cursor-based over a stable catalogue: concatenating pages yields the
            unpaged result exactly once, in the same order; the final page has
            next_cursor null."
    checked_by: [LP-10, LP-11, LP-12]
  R-10:
    text: "The cursor is opaque and encodes the filter/sort it was produced under. `limit`
            may change between pages; any other divergence is rejected."
    checked_by: [LP-13]
  R-11:
    text: "Rejections are 400 with body {error:{code,message,field}}. Codes:
            invalid_limit, invalid_cursor, invalid_sort, cursor_query_mismatch."
    checked_by: [LP-14, LP-15, LP-16, LP-17, LP-13]
  R-12:
    text: "Unknown query parameters are ignored, not rejected."
    checked_by: [LP-18]
  R-13:
    text: "Any method other than GET on the collection is 405 with an Allow header."
    checked_by: [LP-19]
  R-C1:
    text: "The client sends exactly the parameters the caller supplied. Omitted arguments
            produce no query parameter; defaults are the server's to apply."
    checked_by: [LP-01, LP-20]
  R-C2:
    text: "The client performs no local validation: out-of-range arguments are transmitted
            and the server's rejection is surfaced."
    checked_by: [LP-14]
  R-C3:
    text: "has_more is next_cursor != null."
    checked_by: [LP-10, LP-12]
  R-C4:
    text: "Unknown fields in a 200 body are ignored, not an error."
    checked_by: [LP-21]
  R-C5:
    text: "A 2xx body that is not decodable as {items, next_cursor} is ProtocolError, and
            no partial page is returned."
    checked_by: [LP-22]
  R-C6:
    text: "503 is retried once after the interval in Retry-After; a second 503 raises
            ServerError. 4xx is never retried."
    checked_by: [LP-23, LP-24]
  R-C7:
    text: "The client always sends Accept: application/json."
    checked_by: [LP-01]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Cases
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
cases:

  - id: LP-01

    fixture: catalog_A

I chose a declarative data contract rather than prose or Gherkin because every case here is already a four-part record — client call in, HTTP request out, HTTP response in, client result out — which lets the server harness read the middle two fields and the client harness read all four, so a single row verifies both sides and no second copy is needed. YAML specifically because it diffs cleanly in review, carries the explanatory comments that a JSON contract would lose, and needs no parser beyond what both stacks already have. The small matcher vocabulary (`$opaque`/`$bound`/`$contains`/`$product`) exists so genuinely unspecified values like cursors and error messages stay unspecified while remaining machine-checkable, instead of being frozen into the spec by accident. The `rules` block with `checked_by` back-references makes coverage itself a test: an unchecked rule fails the build, which is what stops this file from drifting into documentation.

  Rule: Filtering, sorting and pagination compose

    Scenario: Combining a category filter with descending sort and paging
      When I list products filtered by category "Kitchen", sorted by "price" descending, with pageSize 2 and page 1

```

I chose Gherkin because it is a plain-text, tool-agnostic format expressly built for one specification to be executed by many independent step-definition suites, which matches "one file, two implementations" exactly. Its Given/When/Then structure naturally expresses externally observable behavior rather than internals, keeping the spec honest as a black-box contract. Being human-readable, it also doubles as living documentation that a non-programmer can review. Finally, mature runners exist for virtually any language (Cucumber-JVM, cucumber-js, Behave, SpecFlow), so the server and client teams can each bind the same file in their own stack without ever forking its content.
